claim: RNA sequencing identified 604 genes that are significantly up- or down-regulated by cold-warming conditions (2 hrs exposure to 4°C cold shock followed by recovery at 20°C for 1 hr) in wild-type C. elegans.
source: After differential expression analyses of triplicate samples, we identified 604 genes that are significantly up- or down-regulated by such CW conditions (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq experimental data from triplicate samples with differential expression analysis.

claim: Cold-warming regulated genes are involved in biological processes including lipid metabolisms, autophagy, proteostasis and cell signaling.
source: Gene ontology analysis indicates that the CW-regulated genes are involved in biological processes including lipid metabolisms, autophagy, proteostasis and cell signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: asp-17 is a robust CW-inducible reporter gene with low baseline expression level and high-fold induction by CW.
source: In this work, we focus on asp-17 as a robust CW-inducible reporter gene owing to its low baseline expression level and high-fold induction by CW, features that permitted facile isolation of full-penetrance mutants after random mutagenesis (see below) with both abnormal asp-17p::GFP expression and altered organismic tolerance to prolonged cold stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of asp-17 expression characteristics that made it suitable for genetic screening.

claim: C. elegans asp-17 encodes an aspartyl-like protease with unknown molecular functions.
source: C. elegans asp-17 encodes an aspartyl-like protease with unknown molecular functions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the asp-17 gene product.

claim: asp-17 up-regulation is more prominently induced by severe than moderate hypothermia followed by recovery from cold shock.
source: Like other CW-inducible genes, asp-17 up-regulation is more prominently induced by severe than moderate hypothermia followed by recovery from cold shock (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and QPCR data shown in Figure 1B and C comparing different temperature conditions.

claim: Only asp-17 was robustly and specifically induced by CW among the aspartyl-like protease family members.
source: Among the aspartyl-like protease family members, we found that only asp-17 was robustly and specifically induced by CW (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq quantification data shown in Figure 1D comparing asp family gene expression.

claim: The up-regulation of endogenous asp-17 by CW can be recapitulated by an integrated GFP reporter driven by the endogenous asp-17 promoter.
source: The up-regulation of endogenous asp-17 by CW can be recapitulated by an integrated GFP reporter driven by the endogenous asp-17 promoter, indicating transcriptional regulation of asp-17 by CW (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data of the asp-17p::GFP reporter shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The induction of asp-17 strictly required the warming phase after cold shock.
source: We varied CW treatment conditions and found that the induction of asp-17 strictly required the warming phase after cold shock (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR measurements shown in Figure 1E testing different cold and warming durations.

claim: Heat shock at 32°C did not increase asp-17 expression.
source: However, heat shock at 32°C did not increase asp-17 expression (Figure 1E), consistent with previous large-scale transcriptome profiling studies in C. elegans (Brunquell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data in Figure 1E and is consistent with published transcriptome studies.

claim: CW-induced asp-17 is predominantly expressed in intestinal cells.
source: Single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH) identified the CW-induced asp-17 predominantly in intestinal cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Over 30 mutants with constitutive asp-17p::GFP expression were isolated from EMS-induced random mutagenesis screen.
source: We performed a forward genetic screen using EMS-induced random mutagenesis of a parental strain carrying a genome-integrated asp-17p::GFP reporter and isolated over 30 mutants with constitutive asp-17p::GFP expression in the absence of CW (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the genetic screen results documented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The dma50 mutant exhibited fully penetrant and constitutively strong expression of asp-17p::GFP.
source: We molecularly cloned one mutant dma50 that exhibited fully penetrant and constitutively strong expression of asp-17p::GFP (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and genetic mapping data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–1F.

claim: dma50 strongly up-regulated asp-17::GFP in the intestine compared with wild type.
source: Compared with wild type, dma50 strongly up-regulated asp-17::GFP in the intestine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: dma50 defines a previously uncharacterized C. elegans gene isy-1.
source: Based on phenocopying by feeding RNAi against the candidate genes and transformation rescue of the asp-17p::GFP phenotype, dma50 defines a previously uncharacterized C. elegans gene isy-1 (Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic mapping, RNAi phenocopying, and rescue experiments shown in Figure 2A–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: isy-1 (Interactor of SYF1 in yeast) encodes a protein with strong sequence similarity to an evolutionarily highly conserved family of RNA-binding proteins in eukaryotes.
source: isy-1 (Interactor of SYF1 in yeast) encodes a protein with strong sequence similarity to an evolutionarily highly conserved family of RNA-binding proteins in eukaryotes (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C) (Dix et al., 1999; Du et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C, and by citations to previous studies.

claim: dma50 caused substitution of a negatively charged glutamate to a positively charged lysine in the predicted coiled-coil region of C. elegans ISY-1.
source: dma50 caused substitution of a negatively charged glutamate, which is completely conserved in the ISY protein family, to a positively charged lysine in the predicted coiled-coil region of C. elegans ISY-1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and mutation identification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The glutamate residue substituted by dma50 is completely conserved in the ISY protein family.
source: dma50 caused substitution of a negatively charged glutamate, which is completely conserved in the ISY protein family, to a positively charged lysine in the predicted coiled-coil region of C. elegans ISY-1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ISY-1::GFP is distributed ubiquitously in many tissues including intestinal nuclei.
source: An isy-1p::isy-1::GFP translational reporter indicated a rather ubiquitous distribution of ISY-1::GFP in many tissues including intestinal nuclei (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of the ISY-1::GFP reporter shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The strong intestinal asp-17p::GFP expression caused by dma50 was fully rescued by transgenic expression of wild-type isy-1(+).
source: The strong intestinal asp-17p::GFP expression caused by dma50 was fully rescued by transgenic expression of wild-type isy-1(+), single-copy integration of a mCherry-tagged isy-1(+) allele, or isy-1(+) expression driven by the intestine-specific ges-1 promoter (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The ges-1-driven transgenic expression of sense plus antisense isy-1 RNAi fully recapitulated the dma50 phenotype.
source: In addition, the ges-1-driven transgenic expression of sense plus antisense isy-1 RNAi fully recapitulated the dma50 phenotype (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Endogenous expression of asp-17 was drastically up-regulated in isy-1 mutants.
source: Endogenous expression of asp-17 was also drastically up-regulated in isy-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: isy-1 is a causal cell-autonomous regulator of asp-17.
source: Thus, these results identify isy-1 as a causal cell-autonomous regulator of asp-17.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments and tissue-specific RNAi results presented.

claim: Human ISY1 is critical for certain microRNA processing.
source: Human ISY1 is critical for certain microRNA processing while yeast ISY1 is a likely component of the spliceosome (Dix et al., 1999; Du et al., 2015; Galej et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast ISY1 is a likely component of the spliceosome.
source: Human ISY1 is critical for certain microRNA processing while yeast ISY1 is a likely component of the spliceosome (Dix et al., 1999; Du et al., 2015; Galej et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CW-induced asp-17 up-regulation was further enhanced in isy-1 mutants compared with wild type.
source: We found that CW-induced asp-17 up-regulation was further enhanced in isy-1 mutants compared with wild type (Figure 3A), suggesting that ISY-1 normally restricts transcriptional activity of asp-17.
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ISY-1 normally restricts transcriptional activity of asp-17.
source: We found that CW-induced asp-17 up-regulation was further enhanced in isy-1 mutants compared with wild type (Figure 3A), suggesting that ISY-1 normally restricts transcriptional activity of asp-17.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that isy-1 mutants show enhanced asp-17 expression.

claim: zip-10 encodes a bZIP-type transcription factor.
source: We performed RNA-seq from triplicate samples of wild-type hermaphrodites and isy-1 mutants, from which we analyzed differentially expressed TF-encoding genes in isy-1 mutants and found that a bZIP-type transcription factor-encoding gene zip-10 met both criteria (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and gene annotation.

claim: zip-10 mRNA was drastically up-regulated in isy-1 mutants.
source: zip-10 mRNA was drastically up-regulated in isy-1 mutants, whereas levels of closely related bZIP family genes, such as zip-11, were unaffected (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Levels of closely related bZIP family genes, such as zip-11, were unaffected in isy-1 mutants.
source: zip-10 mRNA was drastically up-regulated in isy-1 mutants, whereas levels of closely related bZIP family genes, such as zip-11, were unaffected (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genetic deletion of zip-10 completely abrogated the ability of isy-1 RNAi to activate asp-17p::GFP.
source: Importantly, genetic deletion of zip-10 completely abrogated the ability of isy-1 RNAi to activate asp-17p::GFP (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ISY-1 regulates asp-17 by controlling the level of zip-10 mRNAs.
source: These results indicate that ISY-1 regulates asp-17 by controlling the level of zip-10 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis and expression data presented.

claim: CW did not apparently alter levels of endogenous isy-1 mRNAs.
source: CW did not apparently alter levels of endogenous isy-1 mRNAs or mCherry-tagged ISY-1 proteins under the endogenous isy-1 promoter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: CW did not apparently alter levels of mCherry-tagged ISY-1 proteins under the endogenous isy-1 promoter.
source: CW did not apparently alter levels of endogenous isy-1 mRNAs or mCherry-tagged ISY-1 proteins under the endogenous isy-1 promoter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CW induced drastic up-regulation of ZIP-10 proteins from a tagged zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG allele.
source: By contrast, we found that CW induced drastic up-regulation of ZIP-10 proteins from a tagged zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG allele in an integrated transgenic strain (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The induction of ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG was completely blocked by RNAi against zip-10 or GFP.
source: Although EGFP fluorescence was invisible in animals carrying such transgenes (likely because it is sandwiched by zip-10 and FLAG), the striking induction of ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG was completely blocked by RNAi against zip-10 or GFP, confirming the transgene specificity (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The baseline level of ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG was close to the detection limit of western blot under normal conditions.
source: The baseline level of ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG was close to the detection limit of western blot under normal conditions, but nonetheless is strongly up-regulated upon RNAi against isy-1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG is strongly up-regulated upon RNAi against isy-1.
source: The baseline level of ZIP-10::EGFP::FLAG was close to the detection limit of western blot under normal conditions, but nonetheless is strongly up-regulated upon RNAi against isy-1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The induction of zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG strictly required the warming phase of CW.
source: Similar to that of asp-17, the induction of zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG strictly required the warming phase of CW and occurred rapidly but transiently after warming during CW (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The induction of zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG occurred rapidly but transiently after warming during CW.
source: Similar to that of asp-17, the induction of zip-10p::zip-10::EGFP::FLAG strictly required the warming phase of CW and occurred rapidly but transiently after warming during CW (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CW strongly up-regulated asp-17 expression in both wild type and isy-1 mutants.
source: CW strongly up-regulated asp-17 expression in both wild type and isy-1 mutants, which exhibited abnormally high zip-10 mRNA levels (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: zip-10 deletion completely abrogated the up-regulation of asp-17 levels by CW.
source: Furthermore, zip-10 deletion completely abrogated the up-regulation of asp-17 levels by CW (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: cpr-3 requires ZIP-10 for CW induction.
source: We also examined the ZIP-10 dependency of other CW-inducible genes identified by RNA-seq and found that at least cpr-3 also required ZIP-10, but other CW-inducible genes including srr-6 and F53A9.1, did not (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CW-inducible genes srr-6 and F53A9.1 do not require ZIP-10.
source: We also examined the ZIP-10 dependency of other CW-inducible genes identified by RNA-seq and found that at least cpr-3 also required ZIP-10, but other CW-inducible genes including srr-6 and F53A9.1, did not (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: ISY-1 suppresses asp-17 by decreasing zip-10 levels.
source: These results demonstrate that ISY-1 suppresses asp-17 by decreasing zip-10 levels whereas CW up-regulates ZIP-10 protein abundance to promote asp-17 expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and expression data presented.

claim: CW up-regulates ZIP-10 protein abundance to promote asp-17 expression.
source: These results demonstrate that ISY-1 suppresses asp-17 by decreasing zip-10 levels whereas CW up-regulates ZIP-10 protein abundance to promote asp-17 expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and expression data presented.

claim: Loss of ISY-1 function did not affect general intron splicing based on an intronic GFP reporter assay.
source: Loss of ISY-1 function affected neither general intron splicing, based on an intronic GFP reporter assay, nor specific splicing of zip-10, although both CW and isy-1 mutations strongly up-regulated zip-10 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of ISY-1 function did not affect specific splicing of zip-10.
source: Loss of ISY-1 function affected neither general intron splicing, based on an intronic GFP reporter assay, nor specific splicing of zip-10, although both CW and isy-1 mutations strongly up-regulated zip-10 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Both CW and isy-1 mutations strongly up-regulated zip-10 mRNA levels.
source: Loss of ISY-1 function affected neither general intron splicing, based on an intronic GFP reporter assay, nor specific splicing of zip-10, although both CW and isy-1 mutations strongly up-regulated zip-10 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and QPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: A GFP transcriptional reporter driven by the endogenous zip-10 promoter was markedly up-regulated by isy-1 RNAi.
source: We constructed a GFP transcriptional reporter driven by the endogenous zip-10 promoter and found it was markedly up-regulated by isy-1 RNAi (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Non-thermal stresses such as hypoxia and starvation did not increase ZIP-10 levels.
source: While non-thermal stresses such as hypoxia and starvation did not increase ZIP-10 levels, CW drastically increased abundance of ZIP-10 in both cytosol and nucleus without affecting abundance of other house-keeping proteins, including HSP90, tubulin and histone H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: CW drastically increased abundance of ZIP-10 in both cytosol and nucleus.
source: While non-thermal stresses such as hypoxia and starvation did not increase ZIP-10 levels, CW drastically increased abundance of ZIP-10 in both cytosol and nucleus without affecting abundance of other house-keeping proteins, including HSP90, tubulin and histone H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data of subcellular fractions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CW did not affect abundance of house-keeping proteins including HSP90, tubulin and histone H3.
source: While non-thermal stresses such as hypoxia and starvation did not increase ZIP-10 levels, CW drastically increased abundance of ZIP-10 in both cytosol and nucleus without affecting abundance of other house-keeping proteins, including HSP90, tubulin and histone H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: CW up-regulation of ZIP-10 required warming and was enhanced by more prolonged cold shock.
source: CW up-regulation of ZIP-10 required warming and was enhanced by more prolonged cold shock (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: RNAi against genes encoding eIF5 and a component of the Ccr4-Not complex did not apparently alter ZIP-10 levels.
source: Since CW can markedly increase zip-10 mRNA levels but to a lesser extent than the isy-1 mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E), we tested whether ZIP-10 proteins might be regulated by CW through translational control and mRNA stability. RNAi against genes encoding eIF5 and a component of the Ccr4-Not complex did not apparently alter ZIP-10 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CW and ISY-1 regulate zip-10 primarily at the transcriptional level.
source: Together, these results indicate that CW and ISY-1 regulate zip-10 primarily at the transcriptional level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reporter assays and the lack of evidence for post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: Human ISY1 facilitates the processing of primary transcripts encoding certain families of microRNAs.
source: Human ISY1 facilitates the processing of primary transcripts encoding certain families of microRNAs (Du et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Both zip-10 and asp-17 are up-regulated in a mutant C. elegans strain deficient in the microRNA mir-60.
source: Both zip-10 and asp-17 are up-regulated in a mutant C. elegans strain deficient in the microRNA mir-60 (Kato et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of mCherry-tagged ISY-1 followed by QPCR revealed specific binding of primary transcripts encoding mir-60.
source: Immunoprecipitation of mCherry-tagged ISY-1 followed by quantitative PCR (QPCR) revealed specific binding of primary transcripts encoding mir-60 as well as a protein-coding gene cebp-1 (Figure 4A–4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-QPCR data shown in Figure 4A–4C.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of mCherry-tagged ISY-1 followed by QPCR revealed specific binding of primary transcripts encoding cebp-1.
source: Immunoprecipitation of mCherry-tagged ISY-1 followed by quantitative PCR (QPCR) revealed specific binding of primary transcripts encoding mir-60 as well as a protein-coding gene cebp-1 (Figure 4A–4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-QPCR data shown in Figure 4A–4C.

claim: Neither isy-1 nor mir-60 levels were affected by CW.
source: Although neither isy-1 nor mir-60 levels were affected by CW, we found CW slightly increased mir-60 binding to ISY-1, perhaps as a feedback mechanism to limit over-activation of zip-10-dependent genes after CW treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-QPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CW slightly increased mir-60 binding to ISY-1.
source: Although neither isy-1 nor mir-60 levels were affected by CW, we found CW slightly increased mir-60 binding to ISY-1, perhaps as a feedback mechanism to limit over-activation of zip-10-dependent genes after CW treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RIP-QPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increased mir-60 binding to ISY-1 after CW may be a feedback mechanism to limit over-activation of zip-10-dependent genes.
source: Although neither isy-1 nor mir-60 levels were affected by CW, we found CW slightly increased mir-60 binding to ISY-1, perhaps as a feedback mechanism to limit over-activation of zip-10-dependent genes after CW treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the biological significance of the observed increased binding.

claim: Mature mir-60 levels were drastically decreased in isy-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, mature mir-60 levels were drastically decreased in isy-1 mutants while loss of mir-60 led to up-regulation of zip-10 and zip-10-dependent subset of CW-inducible genes, including asp-17 and cpr-3, but not many other CW-inducible genes (Figure 4D and E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Loss of mir-60 led to up-regulation of zip-10 and zip-10-dependent subset of CW-inducible genes, including asp-17 and cpr-3.
source: Importantly, mature mir-60 levels were drastically decreased in isy-1 mutants while loss of mir-60 led to up-regulation of zip-10 and zip-10-dependent subset of CW-inducible genes, including asp-17 and cpr-3, but not many other CW-inducible genes (Figure 4D and E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Loss of mir-60 did not affect many other CW-inducible genes.
source: Importantly, mature mir-60 levels were drastically decreased in isy-1 mutants while loss of mir-60 led to up-regulation of zip-10 and zip-10-dependent subset of CW-inducible genes, including asp-17 and cpr-3, but not many other CW-inducible genes (Figure 4D and E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The 3' untranslated region (Utr) of zip-10 was not regulated by CW or isy-1 RNAi.
source: The 3' untranslated region (Utr) of zip-10 appeared not to be regulated by CW or isy-1 RNAi (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data of a 3'UTR reporter shown in Figure 4F.

claim: isy-1 RNAi caused an abnormally high baseline level of ZIP-10 in the absence of CW.
source: However, isy-1 RNAi caused an abnormally high baseline level of ZIP-10 in the absence of CW and enabled further heightened ZIP-10 up-regulation in response to CW, followed by its down-regulation over an extended period of warming (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: isy-1 RNAi enabled further heightened ZIP-10 up-regulation in response to CW.
source: However, isy-1 RNAi caused an abnormally high baseline level of ZIP-10 in the absence of CW and enabled further heightened ZIP-10 up-regulation in response to CW, followed by its down-regulation over an extended period of warming (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CW regulates transcription of zip-10 (and thereby that of asp-17).
source: These results indicate that CW regulates transcription of zip-10 (and thereby that of asp-17), while ISY-1 controls expression of zip-10 via mir-60, likely through microRNA processing and regulation of additional upstream transcriptional zip-10 regulators that respond to CW.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on zip-10 and asp-17 regulation.

claim: ISY-1 controls expression of zip-10 via mir-60, likely through microRNA processing and regulation of additional upstream transcriptional zip-10 regulators that respond to CW.
source: These results indicate that CW regulates transcription of zip-10 (and thereby that of asp-17), while ISY-1 controls expression of zip-10 via mir-60, likely through microRNA processing and regulation of additional upstream transcriptional zip-10 regulators that respond to CW.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RIP, QPCR, and genetic data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: 246 genes are commonly regulated by both CW and isy-1(dma50) mutants.
source: We compared the genes differentially regulated by CW and those by isy-1(dma50) mutants and found 246 genes, including the two ZIP-10-dependent targets asp-17 and cpr-3, that are commonly regulated by both conditions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Global transcriptome changes between CW and isy-1(dma50) conditions are significantly correlated (correlation coefficient R as 0.54, significance P value as 0).
source: Global transcriptome changes between these two conditions are also significantly correlated (Figure 5B) (correlation coefficient R as 0.54, significance P value as 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 5B with statistical correlation analysis.

claim: A single enriched motif characterized by AT-rich sequences was identified in the promoters of commonly regulated genes by CW and isy-1.
source: We used the bioinformatics tool MEME (Bailey et al., 2009) to identify motifs present in the promoters (~600 bp upstream of transcription start sites) of the commonly regulated gene subset and identified a single enriched motif characterized by AT-rich sequences (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEME motif analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The gene most enriched with the AT-rich motif is asp-17, which contains 16 such motifs in its promoter.
source: The gene most enriched with this motif is asp-17, the promoter of which contains 16 such motifs (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ZIP-10 is a bZIP-type transcription factor predicted to contain N-terminal low sequence-complexity domains and a C-terminal DNA-binding and glutamine-rich transactivation domain.
source: ZIP-10 is a bZIP-type transcription factor predicted to contain N-terminal low sequence-complexity domains and a C-terminal DNA-binding and glutamine-rich transactivation domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–H.

claim: ChIP experiments detected asp-17 promoter sequences in the FLAG-tagged ZIP-10 chromatin complex only under CW conditions.
source: To test whether the asp-17 promoter with the identified AT-rich motifs can be bound directly by ZIP-10, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) experiments and detected asp-17 promoter sequences in the FLAG-tagged ZIP-10 chromatin complex only under CW conditions (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-QPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ZIP-10 directly binds to and activates the asp-17 promoter in the genetic program regulated by ISY-1 and CW.
source: These results indicate that ZIP-10 directly binds to and activates the asp-17 promoter in the genetic program regulated by ISY-1 and CW.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ChIP data and the genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: asp-17 or zip-10 loss-of-function mutants exhibited markedly higher survival rates than wild type under prolonged CW stress.
source: We found that asp-17 or zip-10 loss-of-function mutants exhibited markedly higher survival rates than wild type under the same prolonged CW stress condition (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Inducible zip-10 over-expression by mild transient heat shock promoted animal death even in the absence of CW.
source: Consistent with a role of wild-type zip-10 in promoting organismic death, inducible zip-10 over-expression by mild transient heat shock, mediated by the hsp-16 promoter, promoted animal death even in the absence of CW (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by organismic death rate data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Ectopically induced zip-11 and zip-2 did not affect animal death.
source: By contrast, other ectopically induced zip genes including zip-11 and zip-2 did not affect animal death, while a mutation specifically disrupting the glutamine-rich transactivation domain of ZIP-10 abolished the death-promoting effect (Figure 5F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by organismic death rate data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A mutation specifically disrupting the glutamine-rich transactivation domain of ZIP-10 abolished the death-promoting effect.
source: By contrast, other ectopically induced zip genes including zip-11 and zip-2 did not affect animal death, while a mutation specifically disrupting the glutamine-rich transactivation domain of ZIP-10 abolished the death-promoting effect (Figure 5F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by organismic death rate data shown in Figure 5F and protein sequence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H.

claim: zip-10 is genetically epistatic to isy-1 in the regulation of asp-17.
source: Although zip-10 is genetically epistatic to isy-1 in the regulation of asp-17, we found that isy-1 mutants are also markedly resistant to prolonged cold stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by the genetic epistasis data presented earlier (Figure 3D).

claim: isy-1 mutants are markedly resistant to prolonged cold stress.
source: Although zip-10 is genetically epistatic to isy-1 in the regulation of asp-17, we found that isy-1 mutants are also markedly resistant to prolonged cold stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data (referenced in the text and shown in Figure 5H).

claim: Many downstream target genes of the stress-coping transcription factors HIF-1, HSF-1 and DAF-16 are up-regulated in isy-1 mutants.
source: This paradox was resolved after we observed that many downstream target genes of the stress-coping transcription factors HIF-1, HSF-1 and DAF-16 are up-regulated in isy-1 mutants, and LOF of at least daf-16 could partly suppress cold tolerance by isy-1 RNAi (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: LOF of daf-16 could partly suppress cold tolerance by isy-1 RNAi.
source: This paradox was resolved after we observed that many downstream target genes of the stress-coping transcription factors HIF-1, HSF-1 and DAF-16 are up-regulated in isy-1 mutants, and LOF of at least daf-16 could partly suppress cold tolerance by isy-1 RNAi (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Small RNA library sequencing identified specific members of microRNAs that were differentially regulated in isy-1 mutants, including mir-60 and additional microRNAs predicted to target stress-coping TFs.
source: Since ISY-1 regulates zip-10 via mir-60 (Figure 4) supporting a role of ISY-1 in specific microRNA processing (Du et al., 2015), we performed small RNA library sequencing of wild type animals and isy-1 mutants and identified specific members of microRNAs that were differentially regulated, including mir-60 and additional microRNAs predicted to target stress-coping TFs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: isy-1 mutants likely exhibit pleiotropic phenotypes caused by abnormal activation of multiple TFs in addition to ZIP-10.
source: Thus, isy-1 mutants likely exhibit pleiotropic phenotypes caused by abnormal activation of multiple TFs in addition to ZIP-10.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that multiple TF targets are affected in isy-1 mutants.

claim: The HIF-1/HSF-1/DAF-16 target genes were not apparently induced by CW.
source: In contrast to ZIP-10 dependent genes (asp-17 and cpr-3), the HIF-1/HSF-1/DAF-16 target genes were not apparently induced by CW (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: ZIP-10 is more strongly induced by CW in adults than in larvae.
source: Furthermore, unlike HSF-1 or DAF-16 that are induced by other types of stress stimuli, ZIP-10 is more strongly induced by CW in adults than in larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), suggesting phenoptosis-promoting effects of zip-10 more specifically for adults.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The phenotypic difference in cold tolerance between wild type animals and zip-10 mutants manifested more prominently in developmentally more mature-stage and older animals.
source: Indeed, the phenotypic difference in cold tolerance between wild type animals and zip-10 mutants manifested more prominently in developmentally more mature-stage and older animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data at different developmental stages shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: CW specifically activates a ZIP-10-driven and developmental stage-modulated transcriptional genetic program to promote the organismic death, or phenoptosis, of C. elegans.
source: These results indicate that CW specifically activates a ZIP-10-driven and developmental stage-modulated transcriptional genetic program to promote the organismic death, or phenoptosis, of C. elegans (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined genetic, expression, and survival data presented.

claim: Identified transcriptional targets of ZIP-10 include at least two Cathepsin-type proteases, CPR-3 and ASP-17.
source: However, unlike other stress-responding TFs that activate genes largely beneficial for physiological homeostasis and thus animal health under stress conditions (Baird et al., 2014; Dempersmier et al., 2015; Hwang and Lee, 2011; Kandror et al., 2004; Kumsta et al., 2017; Landis and Murphy, 2010), identified transcriptional targets of ZIP-10 include at least two Cathepsin-type proteases, CPR-3 and ASP-17 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CPR-4, a Cathepsin CPR-3 paralogue, has been shown to inhibit cell deaths in C. elegans.
source: In contrast to aspartyl-type proteases which are largely unknown in cellular functions, caspase-type proteases are well-known apoptotic cell death executioners while CPR-4, a Cathepsin CPR-3 paralogue, has been shown to inhibit cell deaths in C. elegans (Metzstein et al., 1998; Peng et al., 2017; Peter, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Caspase-type proteases are well-known apoptotic cell death executioners.
source: In contrast to aspartyl-type proteases which are largely unknown in cellular functions, caspase-type proteases are well-known apoptotic cell death executioners while CPR-4, a Cathepsin CPR-3 paralogue, has been shown to inhibit cell deaths in C. elegans (Metzstein et al., 1998; Peng et al., 2017; Peter, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of zip-10 and its targets promotes organismic deaths.
source: Ectopic expression of zip-10 and its targets promotes organismic deaths, in contrast to the effect of zip-10 or asp-17 deficiency on cold tolerance (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by organismic death rate data shown in Figure 5F and survival data in Figure 5E.

claim: The pro-death role of the zip-10 genetic program likely depends on multiple factors, including the duration and severity of cold exposure.
source: As duration of cold shock affects levels of ZIP-10 and transient CW does not trigger phenoptosis, the pro-death role of the zip-10 genetic program likely depends on multiple factors, including the duration and severity of cold exposure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations about ZIP-10 regulation and phenoptosis.

claim: Apoptotic cell death-promoting effects have been described for specific members of mammalian bZIP TFs.
source: Notably, apoptotic cell death-promoting effects have also been described for specific members of mammalian bZIP TFs (Chüeh et al., 2017; Hartman et al., 2004; Ritchie et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The zip-10 promoter activity responds to the loss of ISY-1.
source: We found that the zip-10 promoter activity responds to the loss of ISY-1, which normally maintains mir-60 levels and thereby regulates zip-10 transcription likely through the processing of small RNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the reporter assay data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claim: ISY-1 normally maintains mir-60 levels and thereby regulates zip-10 transcription likely through the processing of small RNAs.
source: We found that the zip-10 promoter activity responds to the loss of ISY-1, which normally maintains mir-60 levels and thereby regulates zip-10 transcription likely through the processing of small RNAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RIP, QPCR, and small RNA-seq data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Severe cold stress leads to accumulation of another class of small RNA risiRNA, which is important for maintaining rRNA homeostasis.
source: Severe cold stress also leads to accumulation of another class of small RNA risiRNA, which is important for maintaining rRNA homeostasis (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Constitutive up-regulation of ZIP-10 targets in isy-1 mutants and the lack of evidence for regulation of ISY-1 by CW supports ISY-1 as a gate-keeper for the ZIP-10-driven transcriptional response to CW.
source: Constitutive up-regulation of ZIP-10 targets in isy-1 mutants and the lack of evidence for regulation of ISY-1 by CW supports ISY-1 as a gate-keeper for the ZIP-10-driven transcriptional response to CW (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression data and the model shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Regulation of zip-10 is primarily transcriptional.
source: Regulation of zip-10 is primarily transcriptional based on evidence we present in this study; further studies are required to discern to what extent mir-60 might directly act at the zip-10 locus or more indirectly impact the transcription of zip-10, e.g. by post-transcriptionally inhibiting translation of a transcriptional activator.
evidence: The claim is supported by the reporter and expression data presented.

claim: Up-regulation of the activity of the zip-10 promoter by CW indicates that additional cold-responding sensors and effectors upstream of ZIP-10 remain to be identified.
source: Up-regulation of the activity of the zip-10 promoter by CW indicates that additional cold-responding sensors and effectors upstream of ZIP-10 remain to be identified, by signaling mechanisms perhaps similar to the well-characterized cold-responding pathways found in other organisms (Dempersmier et al., 2015; Kandror et al., 2004; Zhu, 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that zip-10 promoter responds to CW, with speculation about unknown upstream regulators.

claim: The roles of ZIP-10 and a dedicated genetic program in promoting organismic death would make sense in light of the evolutionary kin selection theory.
source: The roles of ZIP-10 and a dedicated genetic program in promoting organismic death are surprising but would make sense in light of the evolutionary kin selection theory.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: Kin selection refers to the evolutionary process promoting the reproductive success of an organism's kin despite a cost to the organism's own reproduction.
source: Kin selection refers to the evolutionary process promoting the reproductive success of an organism's kin despite a cost to the organism's own reproduction (Hamilton, 1963; Smith, 1964).
evidence: The claim is based on established evolutionary theory and supported by citations.

claim: Examples of kin selection and stress-induced organismic deterioration have been widely documented in many organisms.
source: Although the concept and potential mechanisms of programed organismic death, or phenoptosis, are debated, examples of kin selection and stress-induced organismic deterioration have been widely documented in many organisms (Longo et al., 2005; Sapolsky, 2004; Skulachev, 1999; 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Laboratory conditions for hermaphroditic C. elegans no longer exert selection pressure for genetic programs underlying phenoptosis or kin selection.
source: Laboratory conditions for hermaphroditic C. elegans clearly no longer exert selection pressure for genetic programs underlying phenoptosis or kin selection.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about laboratory culture conditions.

claim: Mathematical modeling of population growth for wild-type and zip-10 deficient animals under food-limiting and CW stress conditions supports the phenoptosis or kin selection hypothesis for the zip-10 pathway.
source: However, our mathematic modeling of an exemplar situation of population growth for wild-type and zip-10 deficient animals under food-limiting and CW stress conditions supports the phenoptosis or kin selection hypothesis for the zip-10 pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Both the CW-induced zip-10 expression and the death-promoting effect of ZIP-10 occurred more prominently in older adults than in larvae.
source: Experimentally, we found that both the CW-induced zip-10 expression and the death-promoting effect of ZIP-10 occurred more prominently in older adults than in larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and survival assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The evolutionary advantage of programmed organismic death might manifest in the wild, where resources for growth and reproduction are limited and environments can change drastically.
source: Extending from the kin selection theory, we postulate that the evolutionary advantage of programmed organismic death might manifest in the wild, where resources for growth and reproduction are limited and environments can change drastically.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about evolutionary advantages.

claim: The selective death of adult animals would benefit young and reproductively more privileged populations to facilitate the spreading of genes by young populations under resource-limiting and high-stress conditions.
source: As such, the selective death of adult animals would benefit young and reproductively more privileged populations to facilitate the spreading of genes by young populations under resource-limiting and high-stress conditions.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the evolutionary benefit of phenoptosis.

claim: This work provides an unprecedented example of stress-induced phenoptosis in C. elegans.
source: Our work provides an unprecedented example of stress-induced phenoptosis in C. elegans and identify a specific transcription factor in a genetic program that likely evolved to promote kin selection during animal evolution.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in the study.

claim: This work identifies a specific transcription factor (ZIP-10) in a genetic program that likely evolved to promote kin selection during animal evolution.
source: Our work provides an unprecedented example of stress-induced phenoptosis in C. elegans and identify a specific transcription factor in a genetic program that likely evolved to promote kin selection during animal evolution.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings with speculation about evolutionary significance.

claim: Heat shock stimuli activate expression of many heat-shock inducible genes through the sigma-32 factor in bacteria.
source: Heat shock stimuli activate expression of many heat-shock inducible genes through the sigma-32 factor and the evolutionarily conserved transcription factor HSF (Heat Shock Factor) in bacteria and eukaryotes, respectively (Gomez-Pastor et al., 2018; Yura et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Heat shock stimuli activate expression of many heat-shock inducible genes through the evolutionarily conserved transcription factor HSF (Heat Shock Factor) in eukaryotes.
source: Heat shock stimuli activate expression of many heat-shock inducible genes through the sigma-32 factor and the evolutionarily conserved transcription factor HSF (Heat Shock Factor) in bacteria and eukaryotes, respectively (Gomez-Pastor et al., 2018; Yura et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Coordinated expression of heat shock-induced chaperone proteins facilitates cellular proteostasis and adaptation to temperature upshift.
source: Coordinated expression of heat shock-induced chaperone proteins facilitates cellular proteostasis and adaptation to temperature upshift (Mahat et al., 2016; Solís et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: How organisms respond to cold shock is still largely unknown.
source: In contrast to heat shock response, how organisms respond to cold shock is still largely unknown (Al-Fageeh and Smales, 2006; Choi et al., 2012; Yenari and Han, 2012; Zhu, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on the state of scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Master regulators of cold shock response and cold-regulated genes (counterparts of HSF) have long been elusive.
source: Although extensive RNA expression profiling studies have identified many protein-coding genes and non-coding RNAs that are regulated by cold shock via both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms (Al-Fageeh and Smales, 2006; Giuliodori et al., 2010; Kandror et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2017), master regulators of cold shock response and cold-regulated genes (counterparts of HSF) have long been elusive and mechanisms of cold shock response in multicellular organisms remain poorly characterized.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Mechanisms of cold shock response in multicellular organisms remain poorly characterized.
source: Although extensive RNA expression profiling studies have identified many protein-coding genes and non-coding RNAs that are regulated by cold shock via both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms (Al-Fageeh and Smales, 2006; Giuliodori et al., 2010; Kandror et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2017), master regulators of cold shock response and cold-regulated genes (counterparts of HSF) have long been elusive and mechanisms of cold shock response in multicellular organisms remain poorly characterized.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Warm-blooded mammals normally keep body temperature at about 37°C.
source: At the organismic level, warm-blooded mammals normally keep body temperature at about 37°C and initiate multiple homeostatic mechanisms to maintain body temperature upon exposure to hypothermia (Bautista, 2015; Morrison, 2016; Tansey and Johnson, 2015; Vriens et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Therapeutic hypothermia (32–34°C) has been widely used to treat ischemic disorders.
source: In humans, therapeutic hypothermia (32–34°C) has been widely used to treat ischemic disorders and proposed to activate multifaceted cellular programs to protect against ischemic damages (Choi et al., 2012; Polderman, 2009; Yenari and Han, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established medical practice and supported by citations.

claim: Cold-blooded animals including most invertebrates experience varying body temperature depending on the environment.
source: By contrast, cold-blooded animals including most invertebrates experience varying body temperature depending on the environment, but can nonetheless elicit stereotypic behavioral, physiological and transcriptional response to chronic hypothermia or transient cold shock (Al-Fageeh and Smales, 2006; Garrity et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Prolonged severe hypothermia can lead to the death of organisms, in most cases likely because of failure in adapting to the stress, or alternatively through stress-induced phenoptosis.
source: Like many other types of stress, prolonged severe hypothermia can lead to the death of organisms, in most cases likely because of failure in adapting to the stress, or alternatively through stress-induced phenoptosis, namely genetically programed organismic death (Longo et al., 2005; Skulachev, 1999; 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by citations, with speculation about mechanisms.

claim: A C. elegans genetic pathway maintains cell membrane fluidity by regulating lipid desaturation in response to moderate hypothermia (10–15°C).
source: We previously discovered a C. elegans genetic pathway that maintains cell membrane fluidity by regulating lipid desaturation in response to moderate hypothermia (10–15°C) (Fan and Evans, 2015; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Expression of the gene fat-7, which encodes a lipid desaturase, is transcriptionally induced by 10–15°C but not by more severe hypothermia (i.e. cold shock at 0–4°C).
source: Expression of the gene fat-7, which encodes a lipid desaturase, is transcriptionally induced by 10–15°C but not by more severe hypothermia (i.e. cold shock at 0–4°C), which impairs C. elegans reproduction and growth, and elicits distinct physiological and behavioral responses (Garrity et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 1975; Ma et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Severe hypothermia (0–4°C) impairs C. elegans reproduction and growth, and elicits distinct physiological and behavioral responses.
source: Expression of the gene fat-7, which encodes a lipid desaturase, is transcriptionally induced by 10–15°C but not by more severe hypothermia (i.e. cold shock at 0–4°C), which impairs C. elegans reproduction and growth, and elicits distinct physiological and behavioral responses (Garrity et al., 2010; Lyons et al., 1975; Ma et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Strong transcriptional responses to cold shock e.g. 0–4°C likely only manifest during the organismic recovery to normal ambient temperature.
source: However, as severe hypothermia arrests most of cell biological processes, strong transcriptional responses to cold shock e.g. 0–4°C likely only manifest during the organismic recovery to normal ambient temperature.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the understanding of how severe hypothermia affects cellular processes.
